newsitem.title: POLAND: Floods wreak more havoc in Poland, Czech Republic.
newsitem.headline: Floods wreak more havoc in Poland, Czech Republic.

text.p: Raging floodwaters wreaked more havoc in central Europe on Saturday, menacing a historic Polish city centre and driving tens of thousands from their homes in Poland and the Czech Republic.

The region's worst flooding this century has taken more than 50 lives in the two countries and 3,500 sq km (2,170 sq miles) of Poland now lie under water owing to floods that have also ravaged swathes of the eastern Czech Republic.
A surge of high water raging north along the Odra River from flooded southern Poland swamped suburbs of Wroclaw and menaced the historic city centre.

A local government spokesman said authorities were moving to blow breaches in flood walls to free some water and save the centre from the horror already endured by some 50 Polish towns and 300 villages.
The floods caused by heavy rains throughout much of this week have taken at least 26 lives in Poland, police said. Tens of thousands of Poles have been evacuated, leaving deserted villages.
Surging floodwaters drove thousands more villagers in the eastern Czech Republic from their homes on Saturday as officials put the confirmed death toll there at 26.

Some 10,000 people were evacuated from nine villages in the Uherske Hradiste region, close to the Slovak border, as the flood wave which has wrought havoc in the north and east of the country poured south.

About 600 patients, including mothers with newborn babies, were moved from the Uherske Hradiste hospital in an operation involving 1,000 rescue workers, local flood committee spokesman Jaroslav Hrabec said.
The central flood commission said 26 people had lost their lives so far, CTK news agency reported. Three others are still missing, the agency quoted a crisis centre spokeswoman as saying.
In communities just upstream of Wroclaw in Poland, water poured over defences and quickly reached the first storey of buildings, sending residents to upper floors or rooftops to await rescue.

Reuter photographer Pawel Kopczynski, on the scene, said waters in central Wroclaw almost touched the bridges and teams of workers were frantically laying sandbags to protect the low-lying Tumski island with its valuable old buildings. Precious books and archives were being hastily removed from a university library there.
In the suburban community of Korzanow the fast, filthy waters lapped at the base of 10-storey apartment blocs. The water was one or two metres deep in places.
The surge along the Odra and the Wisla caused the capital Warsaw to declare a flood alert.
Although forecasts said the tide was unlikely to spill over when it hit Warsaw early on Monday, the zoo by the Wisla made preparations to safeguard its animals.
Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz has said his government was considering borrowing abroad to help victims and was in talks with the World Bank on a loan.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Bonn had made 400,000 marks ($224,000) available to help the victims of Poland's flooding. He said a convoy with emergency generators, pumps, blankets and drinking water would set off for the Wroclaw area on Saturday.
In the Czech city of Ostrava, staff of the State Scientific Library sought to save thousands of soaked books and documents using hair dryers, CTK reported.

Anxious to avoid delays in rebuilding wrecked roads, bridges and houses, the Czech parliament on Friday to approved the issue of up to five billion crowns ($150 million) in bonds to fund emergency relief. It also pledged five billion crowns in privatisation proceeds.
